title: English Films and the Missing 17th Century

commenti.body:
>So where is our 17th century *Barry Lyndon*?

You have *The Draughtsman's Contract* (1982) and *Winstanley* (1975).  *Winstanley* is one of the best earnest attempts at authentically capturing pre-industrial Europe, even more so than even *Barry Lyndon*.  It's one of the most commendably historically accurate films out there.  Because it really commits to this conceit, it will feel quite alien to most viewers.

I'd add *The Devils* (1971), which is set in France but is an English language production.  It's a masterpiece in my opinion.

There's also *A Field in England* (2013), *The VVitch* (2015), *The Libertine* (2005), *Witchfinder General* (1968), *Restoration* (1995), *The Lady and the Highwayman* (1989) (corny and overwrought though it is), *Fanny Lye Deliver'd* (2019), *The Black Swan* (1942), and *To Kill a King* (2003).

>The Thirty Years' War from 1618-1648 was among the the most destructive events in European history

In general just very few films cover this topic. To my knowledge only *Queen Christina* (1933) (which I haven't seen), *The Last Valley* (1971), and *Bláznova kronika* (*A Jester's Tale*) (1964) cover this event.  I've seen the latter two and *A Jester's Tale* is off-the-wall brilliant.

So they're certainly out there.  I don't think English-language films set in this century are especially absent.  I'd say *The Draughtsman's Contract*, *Winstanley*, and *The Devils* would most satisfy what you're looking for.  *A Field in England*, *The VVitch*, and *The Libertine* are great as well.

(Of all of the above mentioned films, the only one I haven't seen is *Queen Christina*, so it's the only one I can't recommend for or against.)
I genuinely thank you for this reply, many of these don't even seem to appear on the relevant [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Films_set_in_the_17th_century)

Quite welcome!  

Yes, a bit annoying they're not included in that Wikipedia list.  I mostly just happened upon a lot of these films.

But hope you can find them and enjoy.
*All Is True* is another example of a film set during this century.
Saving this comment. I love learning about this time in history so will enjoy watching these!

I've been watching [films about the British Monarchy ](https://letterboxd.com/jupiterkansas/list/british-monarchy-on-film/detail/)and the 16th century seems to be an era that inspired pirate films and high seas adventures, although very few are historically based. **Captain Blood** does a good job of referencing history for what it is. 

It seems like the War of the Roses, Henry VIII, and Queen Elizabeth get most of the historical attention (thanks no doubt partly to Shakespeare) so maybe the 16th century seems dull in comparison, or perhaps Puritan oppression of the arts had something to do with it. 

You likewise can find very few films about pre-Civil War United States.

Just watched The Devils on my Criterion subscription. Incredibly captivating. Oliver Reed was fantastic. 

I also recently watched Barry Lyndon. One thing I think both shared (besides the wonderful Murray Melvin) is an incredible sense of humor. I think if I was younger my eyes would've glazed over the moment I saw the puffy shirts and tight pantaloons but if you give these movies a chance you can see history as something more alight with humor, stupidity, passion, and base desire than it may seem from the straight orthodox teachings of these periods.

All is true, Anonymous, and Shakespeare in love deal with different ideas about who William Shakespeare might have been. 

I quite enjoy Pocahantas and the New World as a double feature.

There have been a number of adaptations of the Scarlet Letter.

I'm not sure I can recommend any version of the Crucible because I think it was a mistake to show what the girls did in the woods but it fits your criteria.

Looks like you have a lot to watch, now.

Well said!

The first time I watched *Barry Lyndon* I was also struck by the wry humor.  Naturally *The Devils* as well.  Ken Russell's dark humor is after my own heart.

I introduce these films to a lot of my friends, not knowing if the material will click with them, and to my pleasant surprise they love both.

Easy targets here are any Three Musketeers movie. Shakespeare in Love, Anonymous or any Shakespeare movie. Or any “new world” movie including Pocahontas, Terence Malick’s The New World, and I hear there’s a TV show about Jamestown though I haven’t seen it. 

You also have Elizabeth, The Man Who Killed Don Quixote, The Crucible, Girl with a Pearl Earring and The Scarlet Letter. 

There’s the infamously “troubled” box office bomb Cutthroat Island. It’s not terrible!

Well, partially it may be because it was a complicated century for England and a less "successful" one compared to the ones before and after. Thus, given that US filmmakers rarely move away from English history when doing historical movies, there are less movies overall, besides stuff about Louis XIV and the Three Musketeers (of which there are a lot of movies though). At least if we are looking at English-speaking movies, but there are a lot movies set in that century from European countries. Worth noting that the Elizabethan age takes place partially at the beginning of the 17th, so Elizabeth The Golden Age for instance may qualify.

If you're looking for the 17th century's Barry Lyndon I think the only good answer is Roberto Rossellini's La prise de pouvoir par Louis XIV or maybe The New World by Malick if you want something in English.

Because the Dutch dominated the sees back then. Even went on the Thames to steal the biggest warship the English had (Royal Charles). Don't know if English people know this.

So I think it's a period in time the English like to forget about.

Amazing list 

The Devils is an under appreciated classic of
Cinema 

Also adding Benedetta (2021) to the list
I believe that *Shakespeare in Love* is set during the 1590s, so the last decade of the 16th century. As is *Anonymous*.
